To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the encoding of schema congruent information is supported by the activation of preexisting knowledge structures and that this activation is associated with an increase in the strength of memory for the encoded information.
the encoding of schema congruent but unexpected events is associated with a frontal positivity that is correlated with a lower rate of false alarms in the test phase.

1) Congruent exemplars are remembered better than incon-gruent exemplars; 2) Congruent (HT and LT), but not incongruent exemplar words are associated with a SME in the late N400; 3) Congruent LT exemplar words, but not congruent HT exemplar words, are associated with a late positivity; 4) The late positivity correlates with a reduction of false positive memory judgements in the test phase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the processes involved in schema-based encoding and their contribution to the formation of episodic memory.
the role of semantic knowledge structures in the processing and encoding of information.
the question of how activated schemata support memory for congruent information by facilitating the encoding of item details.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the processes involved in the encoding of schema-related information are reflected by SMEs in the N400 and the P600, and that both processes contribute to subsequent memory.
the activation of schemata during encoding facilitates memory by strengthening the representation of schema congruent information and by suppressing the representation of semantically related items.
the processes reflected by frontal positivity are involved in the encoding of unexpected but schema-congruent events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

congruent information is encoded better because it is integrated more strongly into a preexisting schema, and that unexpected information is encoded better when it can be integrated in the context of the schema.
the processes reflected by SME and frontal positivity are involved in the encoding of schema-related information.
the activation of a schema supports the encoding of congruent information by strengthening the encoding of item details and by suppressing the activation of related but irrelevant information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of unexpected events into a schema is not a simple process.
ERPs provide an excellent tool for studying the temporal dynamics of processes that are involved in the encoding of new information.
ERPs recorded during learning can be used to investigate the processes that are involved in the contextual encoding of information.
